source.title: Understanding Emergent Misalignment via Feature Superposition Geometry
source.authors: Gouki Minegishi; Hiroki Furuta; Takeshi Kojima; Yusuke Iwasawa; Yutaka Matsuo

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses SAE feature identification and cosine-similarity analyses in LLMs to test whether internal feature geometry relates to emergent misalignment. This is a different method and setting from the original toy-model account.
record.gate_note: The paper describes a toy-model setup in Appendix B but reports no toy-model results there. Results cited from other papers are not recorded. The filtering experiment is recorded under none because its filtering outcome does not measure a version's named representation claim.
record.test_reason: The study takes superposition as given and uses pretrained SAEs as a tool to explain emergent misalignment. Its results are cosine similarities between selected SAE feature groups (insecure/secure, incorrect/correct advice, toxic), their link to misalignment counts, and a data-filtering method. None of these measures whether features are superposed, whether polysemanticity has a capacity cause, or whether SAEs recover a model's sparse features. The logit-lens and auto-interp checks only validate its own feature selection. The Appendix B toy model is an illustration (Figure 2) with no reported results.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that emergent misalignment arises from feature superposition: fine-tuning on narrow data amplifies nearby harmful features via gradient spillover. They report that geometry-aware filtering reduces misalignment by 34.5%, beats random removal, and slightly beats LLM-as-judge filtering at similar or lower perplexity cost. The superposition link is assumed and correlational, not a test of superposition itself.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than training a small bottleneck toy network and measuring feature geometry across sparsity and importance settings, the study analyzes fine-tuned LLMs using pretrained SAEs, feature correlations, and cosine similarities; it also evaluates dataset filtering.
record.method_sensitivity: The layer-wise analysis reports stronger similarity effects in earlier layers. Training-dynamics analysis focuses on the layer where similarity differences were most pronounced.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE features correlated with misalignment-inducing data (insecure code, incorrect health/career/legal advice) have higher decoder cosine similarity to toxic SAE features than features from normal data. This holds across five LLMs and nearly all layers, and the similarity rises with misaligned-output counts during fine-tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Emergent misalignment occurs when fine-tuning target features lie geometrically near harmful features in SAE dictionary space.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing the half of samples nearest to toxic features cut Gemma-2 2B misaligned outputs from 87 to 57, at PPL 1.7601. Random removal gave 84 (PPL 1.7657) and LLM-as-judge filtering gave 59 (PPL 1.8195). On Gemma-2 9B (Table 6), counts fell from 62 to 27, versus 53 for random removal.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Filtering fine-tuning data by proximity to toxic SAE features reduces emergent misalignment.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The paper treats cosine similarity as a proxy for geometric proximity and for feature expression. The study does not isolate causality between geometry and misalignment in the reported similarity analyses. Most geometry results are plotted without exact values in the text, and no uncertainty estimates are reported. The study relies on pretrained SAEs and does not test whether they recover complete or canonical feature sets.
record.rows_left_out: No reported toy-model outcome was available to record. No rows were omitted for the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: The toy model (5→2 bottleneck, Appendix B) is described only as an illustration. No sparsity transition, geometry or orthogonality results are reported.
Capacity competition and dedicated versus shared dimensions are not examined.
Non-capacity origins of polysemanticity are not examined.
The study uses pretrained SAEs (Gemma Scope, Llama Scope, gpt-oss SAE) without measuring how features spread over neurons or how well SAEs recover sparse features.
SAE feature completeness, stability and canonicality are not tested. The smallest-width SAEs are used by choice.
Linearity and one-dimensionality are assumed. The Limitations section acknowledges multi-dimensional features (Engels et al.) without testing them.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked R1–R16 to V4 and labelled them supports. That is wrong: the study uses SAE features as a tool, and its results concern emergent misalignment, not whether LLMs show superposition or whether SAEs recover features. Figure 5 text contains readable bar values that the reader marked 'figure only'. The Gemma-2 9B filtering result (Table 6: 62 → 53 random, 27 geometry) is unrecorded but does not bear on any version. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: The paper describes a toy model but reports no results testing whether sparse features outnumbering dimensions are stored as overlapping, nearly orthogonal directions, or whether sparsity produces a transition or regular geometry.
The study does not test whether capacity pressure causes polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions while others share.
The study does not test whether polysemanticity can arise without capacity pressure or whether it is evidence of superposition.
It identifies and analyzes SAE features in LLMs, but does not measure how many neurons encode each feature or establish that SAE features are exhaustive.
The study does not test SAE-feature completeness, stability, or canonical status.
The study analyzes decoder directions and their cosine similarities but does not test whether the underlying model features are necessarily one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.
